utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning, technical booth; good morning to the interpreters, the registry staff, the counsel for the Prosecution and for the Defence. Good morning, General Krstic. As you know, we are going to continue with the testimony of witnesses of the Chamber, and we are going to begin with General Halilovic. So, Mr. Usher, can you have the witness brought in. Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. Good morning, my learned friends opposite. With your permission, before Mr. Halilovic comes into the courtroom, the Defence would like to draw the attention of the Chamber to the following fact. Actually, pursuant to a ruling of the Chamber with respect to the witnesses proposed for today, General Halilovic and the second witness, General Hadzihasanovic, the Chamber gave clear instructions as to the time frame, the subject matter, and the circumstances about which the witnesses will be testifying. I don't think there is any need for me to quote from your ruling, because it is quite clear. Briefly, they are to testify about the period immediately prior to the fall of Srebrenica, the fall of Srebrenica, and the movement of the 28th Division during that time period. In view of the fact that yesterday, late in the afternoon, we received some documents referring, in particular, to Witness Hadzihasanovic for the period from 1992 until 1995, which, in form and in content, has been compiled in the form of an expert report, I fear that if we do not abide by your instructions, that we will go outside the scope and frame of the indictment and that we will find ourselves in a situation in which we have been during the past fortnight or so. To be more specific, I think we will find ourself in the same situation as with respect to Exhibit 883, which is being disputed by the parties. Therefore, before we begin the hearing, my objection is intended to request that the parties in the case limit themselves to the time and content envisaged by the ruling of the Trial Chamber dated - allow me to check the date - dated the 15th of December. So I hope Your Honours will give the appropriate instructions to the witness, that he will be asked to testify about those specific circumstances. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, do you have a particular date in mind? The order of the Chamber says before, during, and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the ruling of the Chamber says: "On the presence and role of the 28th Division of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina immediately prior to, during, and immediately after the attack of the Serb forces on that division in July 1995 on the column of people who attempted to leave the Srebrenica enclave during the attack; especially its composition, the weapons at the disposal of the people in the column, what happened to those people in the military sense, and particularly their possible links with the operations that the Bosnian forces conducted in the area of the Tuzla and generally the area under the control of those forces on the breakthroughs possibly made by that column; the number of participants in those breakthroughs; the casualties suffered by the column; the time, as precise as possible, as to when the population learnt about the capture, executions, or the sudden disappearance of people from the column; the general circumstances of the taking of the enclave from the standpoint of the civilian and military authorities of the Muslims at the time of the events." Mr. President, I have interpreted your ruling as specifying an extremely very limited scope of time and events that the witnesses will be called upon to testify about, but under no circumstances do I see it as covering a time period which differs from the document that we have received in this particular case signed by Hadzihasanovic, which covers the period from 1992 to 1995. Rather, this document differs in time from the ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Harmon, do you have any response to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are witnesses who have been summoned by Your Honours. We don't intend to -- attempt to restrict the Court in its questioning of these witnesses. We intend to sit and listen with interest to their testimony. In respect of my colleague's objection, we have no observation at all on it, other than these are your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, just so you're somewhat informed of my viewpoint, it seems to me that the order that we issued which talks about just before or immediately before, whatever the interpretation, is a clause which I would interpret, in light of what's already in the record here, to be the few months before the fall of Srebrenica in order to encompass the kinds of testimony which you have presented, as well as the Prosecution, dealing with what may have been the motivations for Krivaja 95, and what may have been the motivations for what took place. So roughly I would say, from my point of view, it would encompass the early part of the year of 1995 or the several months just before June. But I would have to say that in terms of any discussion of what provoked either side to do what either side did, it may be that one would incidentally have to allude, at least, to the fact that one side thought the other side was violating some agreement which had been arrived at previously. But to that extent, you know, my interpretation would be at least several months before the fall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me also to say that, as you know, Mr. Petrusic, the Defence discussed at length the question of the violation of agreements on demilitarisation. You discussed that at length, so perhaps the Chamber should know what those agreements were, and as you know, those agreements go back to 1993. So all those conditions are very important in terms of understanding the Operation Krivaja 95 and all that preceded the events which are the subject of our discussions. So in my opinion, to limit ourselves to a few days or a few months means limiting our ability to understand the whole. This does not mean that General Krstic is responsible for those things, but in order to understand the facts in the indictment, we need to know what preceded them. But please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour Judge Wald, your suggestions are quite appropriate, and it is only natural that if the Defence during the testimony of General Krstic referred to certain documents issued by General Hadzihasanovic or documents directed to Hadzihasanovic, that both parties should review those documents and ask them to be commented upon by General Hadzihasanovic himself for his understanding of the situation. Also, Mr. President, it seems to me that it is in the interest of establishing the truth that if we have one of the creators and one of the participants on the agreement on demilitarisation, that he should be examined on those circumstances. My principal suggestion or objection, and with respect to these two items, topics, I have nothing to detract or add to what you, Your Honour Judge Wald, have said, but my main concern is that the document which the Defence received yesterday afternoon covers the period 1992 to 1995. We have documents addressed by Hadzihasanovic to the 28th Division, and vice versa. In the assessment of the Defence, this is a military expert report, and that is how it is headed. And if we were to be faced with the tendering of this document, then the whole situation would change. We would have here a document called a military expert report. That is my opinion, Mr. President. We would have a military expert report which would deprive the Defence of the right to put many questions to the witness. But I do agree with you and what Her Honour Judge Wald said regarding the time period and the topics to which these two Generals should testify. Perhaps it would be best for us to proceed, and if the situation so requires, I assume it is our right to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will make one observation, Mr. President. Defence Exhibit 160, which is a military expert report prepared by General Radinovic, covers an area that is well before a few months before. It goes back to 1991. As a matter of fact, in footnote 3 of that report, the first witness is identified. That footnote refers to events in January of 1992. I merely point this out because I think any restriction that the Defence is seeking to impose on Your Honours' ability to inquire goes in the face of evidence that they themselves have presented to Your Honours and which -- about which Your Honours may wish to raise some questions. I only make that observation and point that out to Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. We shall begin. We shall try to focus on the question of Srebrenica, especially with regard to the agreements on demilitarisation, which more or less define the Srebrenica enclave, focusing in particular on that. But we will not be too strict because, as you know, one says that to understand a fact, one has to view it in perspective. But in view of time constraints, we can't go much further than that. So, Mr. Usher, will you please bring the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Halilovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before anything else is said, in view of your past military responsibilities and your current political responsibilities, I should like to ask you whether it is appropriate for me to address you as General, Deputy, or Mr. Minister, or simply as Mr. Halilovic? What do you prefer?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever you find easiest, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps "General Halilovic" is the best. Fine, then. First of all, thank you for coming. I shall now ask you to observe the procedure which I will outline for you. First of all, in answer to questions about identification, could you please spell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: The 6th of January, 1952, in Prijepolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your profession, please?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Currently I'm minister for social welfare policy in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And which is your city of residence?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now living in Sarajevo, Asikovac Street, number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before we begin your examination proper, I should first like to thank you, on behalf of the Chamber, for responding to our summons. I don't doubt that in view of responsibilities, you are a very busy man, and therefore the Chamber will thank you for the information you conveyed to it in your letter of the 23rd of January. I should like to specify for you the framework within which your testimony will fit. You have been called as a Court witness, whereas normally it is the parties that call witnesses to this Tribunal. As the President of the Chamber, it is my duty to indicate to you briefly the conditions under which your examination will take place. In accordance with the solemn declaration you have just taken, you are obliged and expected to tell us the whole truth. The hearing is, in principle, held in public, and we would like to keep it public as much as possible. However, if you should feel it necessary, you can ask the Chamber to make a ruling to go into private session, or even into closed session, which in practice means that during the duration of the private session, the public will not hear your statements, nor any -- and the transcript of your testimony will not be made public. If you have any notes, you may use them to refresh your memory, but we would like to ask you not to read a statement prepared in advance. In accordance with our order issued at the end of December, we ask you to make a spontaneous statement on the facts that you have knowledge of in regard to the attack on the Srebrenica enclave by the Serb forces in July 1994 [as interpreted], the fall of the enclave, and the destiny of its military and civilian population. You may perhaps then be examined by the parties, but it is up to them to decide whether they will do so. Judge Wald draws my attention to the fact that I said 1995. In the transcript it says 1994. As I was saying, the Judges will put questions to you. You may, if you so wish to, not answer a question; however, I must caution you that that is only if your reply may incriminate you. This is Rule 90 (F) of our Rules of Procedure, and even then, the Judges may request you to answer, but what you say may not be used against you later on. We will have a break later on, or maybe earlier if General Krstic needs a break. As President of the Chamber, I wanted to tell you briefly, as the parties would do to their witnesses, what are their duties, what are their rights, how things will evolve, so there we are. We are going to focus on the demilitarise -- on the agreements on demilitarisation and from then on. So please, we ask you now to make your spontaneous statement on the points that we have mentioned for more or less an hour, an hour 20, after which we will have a break. So General Halilovic, we are listening to you.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, allow me to say that I want to make my statement in public. In the letter addressed to you, I indicated the position I held in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, until 8th of June, 1993, I was Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and member of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that period, I was actively in command of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I took part in the negotiations on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa in April and May 1993. From the 8th of June, 1993, the position of the command of the Main Staff was introduced in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I held that position until November the 1st, 1993. From November the 1st, 1993, by decision of the presidency, I was placed at their disposal, and I was no longer in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which means that since November the 1st, 1993, or rather, from that time until the end of the war in 1995, I have been observing the situation on the battlefronts of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a civilian, as a citizen. In view of the position I held in the army and in the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is only natural that I followed closely what was happening in the theatre of war, and especially in Srebrenica. I have read a series of publications, books, newspaper reports, and all other reports that I could get hold of linked to the events in July 1995 in Srebrenica. In my speeches and writings, I was critical of the policies conducted by the state and military leadership of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina because my position was that the moves they were taking on the battlefront, both in political and military terms, were favouring the paramilitary forces of the Bosnian Serbs and the forces coming from Serbia and Montenegro. A series of measures that were taken with respect to the defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially Srebrenica and Zepa, played into the hands of our enemies rather than contributing to the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In my book, I have given five or six arguments or reasons contributing to the fall of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves which fully corresponded to the policy pursued by the political and military leadership of the rebel Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and which suited the aggressor forces against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The basis for the activities of the rebel Bosnian Serbs were the decisions on the strategic goals of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted by the assembly, the so-called assembly of the Serb people in Banja Luka in May 1992, or, to be more precise, on the 12th of May, 1992, and which were published in the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska on the 26th of November, 1993. As they are very brief, allow me to read them out. "The strategic goals or priorities of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina are: One, a state delineation with the other two national communities; two, a corridor between Semberija and Krajina; three, the establishment of a corridor in the Drina River valley."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is most reluctantly that I am objecting, but it is my submission that reference to this Official Gazette of Republika Srpska, the witness is going far beyond the subject matter and the scope of his testimony with regard to the developments in Srebrenica. I hope you will not wrongly interpret the position of the Defence, but I think it would be far more effective if the witness could focus on the events in which he was directly involved in or what he may have heard from other sources, but with special regard to the ruling that you made on the scope of his testimony. I apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, what is your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, this is Your Honours' witnesses. We don't have any observations in respect to Mr. Petrusic's objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Halilovic, perhaps it might be more useful for the Chamber if you were to concentrate on the facts that you participated in as an actor or an observer. We do not wish you to take the position of an expert witness. You are, rather, a fact witness. You told us that you participated in the negotiations on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica. Perhaps you could start with that and then go on to the fall and the developments that followed after the fall of Srebrenica, because we have time constraints, as you know. So if you could focus your testimony on these points, it would be better. In any event, thank you very much for preparing your statement, but if you could go more directly to those points, it would be better.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: If I may, I would just like to quote the third point which relates to Srebrenica and Zepa: "With the establishment of the corridor of the lower flow of the Drina --" the Drina being the river, the borderline river between the two states, between Serb states. I took part in the negotiations on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa in April and May 1993. And for the situation to be clearer to you, to make it clearer, let me say that the operation for the realisation of this third goal, the assembly of the Bosnian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it began in January 1993 at the same time as the attack on the Bosnian Croats on upper Vakuf and the valley of the river Neretva and certain regions of Central Bosnia. The attack was -- they were coordinated by the Serbs and Croats. I would like to remind you of this and then go on to the demilitarisation agreement. On the 16th of April, 1993, there was an attack on the village of Ahmici, that is to say, at the same time when there was fierce fighting for taking over the territory of Konjevic Polje, Kamenica, Srebrenica, Zepa, and so on and so forth. The negotiations took place on the 18th of April at the Sarajevo airport, but before that, it was announced from General Morillon as the commander of UNPROFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 30th of March, 1993, I received a letter which announced that UNPROFOR units were going to be deployed within the Serb enclave - Srebrenica enclave, I'm sorry - and there was initiative for this already in February, and this was given by President Izetbegovic as a sign of goodwill. The first agreement was signed on the 17th of April, 1993, at the Sarajevo airport. I and General Mladic signed it in the presence of General Wahlgren as the UNPROFOR representative. I think that the contents of that agreement is well-known to you and it refers to the urban area of Srebrenica. It states that the demilitarisation will take place within the space of 72 hours and that all weapons, mines, ammunition, and materiel, except medical material, in Srebrenica will be handed over to UNPROFOR under supervision of three officers on each side, and that in the town no person which is armed or any armed unit will remain in town except UNPROFOR. In preparing for this testimony, I must say that I was -- did not have access to any archives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I apologise for interrupting you, but the interpreters are asking that you slow down, please, because they are having difficulty in following you. Please, would you slow down, General. Thank you, but please continue.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I did, however, succeed in coming by one particular document, which was compiled by my deputy, General Jovan Divjak, and which was addressed to the command of the 2nd Corps and the command of Naser Oric in Srebrenica. The document was compiled on the 20th of April, 1993, which testifies to the fact that it was after the agreement of the 17th of April, after the signing of the agreement. Negotiations continued, but at a lower level, not at the level of commanders. General Divjak writes in that document as follows: "I inform you that in the negotiations on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica held on the 19th of April, 1993, no significant steps forward were taken, no significant progress was made. We concretised the fact that the aggressor side outside the contents of the already signed agreement on the demilitarisation of the town of Srebrenica insists that all units on defence lines surrender their weapons, thereby, according to their consents, the area be demilitarised, which is marked by the delineation line." I don't want to read the whole text, but let me, if I may, just read one more paragraph from that text: "UNPROFOR understands by the term 'demilitarisation' - and our side completely agrees with that interpretation - the complete demilitarisation of Srebrenica, and there would be no armed persons except the civilian police and a small section around Srebrenica which can be seen with the naked eye." General Divjak goes on to explain that in Srebrenica there should be no armed persons, soldiers, or reserve policemen, and states that they should be pulled out of the town and that the defence lines should be strengthened. He takes note that we have the absolute support of General Morillon and General Wahlgren, and in one particular sentence he says, and I quote: "Mladic has signed an agreement of that kind, and it is his problem that he doesn't know what it means." Therefore, after the agreement was signed of the 17th of April, paramilitary formations of Bosnian Serbs and aggressors from Serbia and Montenegro did not adhere to the provisions of the signed agreement. After the entry of the Canadian Battalion into Srebrenica, the intensity of combat activity fell off. There was less combat action, but there was sporadic shelling and shooting in the town, at the town, from the surrounding hills. The town was targeted from the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I apologise for interrupting, but perhaps we could go more quickly to what we're interested in. Do you have an idea of what was done to proceed to actual demilitarisation following the agreement? What steps were taken towards demilitarisation following the agreement signed?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: After the agreement, in Srebrenica, in this way, we lost seven to eight additional villages. It is true that the evacuation of the wounded began and that all armed units began to withdraw from the town, as was provided for by the agreement, and that humanitarian aid began to enter the town. On the 4th and 5th of May, there was an all-out attack on Zepa and combat went on until the 7th or 8th of May. After that, we were to meet again at the airport, or more exactly, this meeting took place on the 7th of May. The negotiation went on throughout the night but yielded no results. Mladic asked that all the weapons be handed over to him. General Morillon insisted that the weapons be surrendered to him, or rather, to UNPROFOR, and we ourselves asked that the area of the urban -- the urban area of Srebrenica be demilitarised and that the units be pulled out of the urban area, because Srebrenica and Zepa had already been proclaimed safe areas. On the 8th of May, sometime after midnight - more exactly, around 2.00 a.m. - an agreement was signed on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa, and in the spirit of the negotiations and in the spirit of the agreement that we signed, I informed the command of the 1st and 2nd Corps and, of course, the command of the defence of Srebrenica. The agreement envisaged the withdrawal of the infantry units one and a half kilometres away from the confrontation line, line of contact, which the forces of the Bosnian Serbs never did. The agreement also provided for the withdrawal of artillery and mechanised units of the aggressor, all of them, to certain regions, and that they be placed under the control of UNPROFOR. That too was never respected. The entry of UNPROFOR units into Zepa, the evacuation of the wounded from Zepa was implemented, did take place, and it was said that our units, when leaving the urban area of Srebrenica and Zepa, would evacuate with them overall combat, materiel, and all other equipment and materiel. In the order compiled by our General Staff, it was provided that the units pull out of the urban area of Srebrenica and Zepa, of course with all their weaponry, and that what they were not able to pull out be placed under UNPROFOR control. This agreement, for our part, was complied with to the letter, and after that, from July, that is to say, from May 1993 onwards up until July 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Halilovic, perhaps we could focus a little more closely on June 1995. I think that you mentioned a whole series of sabotage operations by the BH army and, in particular, an operation on the 20th of June, 1995. Do you know who ordered the operation, who issued the orders for that operation, what it consisted of, and what the objectives were, what its targets were? This could perhaps bring us -- throw more light on the fall of Srebrenica itself, give us a better insight into that.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: When we speak of the mistakes made by the Bosnia-Herzegovina republic, its political and military leaders, I'm thinking first and foremost of the fact that they should have liberated -- planned the liberation of Podrinje first, that operation, and only later the other one, Sarajevo one. If they wanted to deblock Sarajevo, measures should have been taken to strengthen the Defence of Srebrenica and Zepa, which, of course, was not resorted to. Secondly, in the spring of 1995, 18 key officers who had command posts at Srebrenica and Zepa were pulled out in order to be trained in Zenica. It would have been logical that at least the 18 officers from the free territory had been sent from Srebrenica to Zepa to train them and to fortify them, to reinforce. Thirdly, an order reached me signed by the Chief of Staff, the representative of the command of the 28th Division in Srebrenica, on diversionary activity during the time of the Sarajevo operation. That order was written on the 20th of June, 1995, and it was signed by the representative of the command of the 28th Division, Major Ramiz Becirevic. Fourth, in view of the fact that we knew what the opposite side was intending, what their strategic interest was in this area, in the Podrinje area, a lot more should have been done towards capacitating and arming the units themselves in Srebrenica and Zepa for a possible defence. And point number five - although there were more reasons, one could have more than five - when the attack on Srebrenica and Zepa took place in July 1995, in my opinion, the Sarajevo operation should have been stopped and all units who were free and capable should have been sent to Srebrenica and Zepa to help the areas that were in jeopardy. And point number six, when the units passed through Srebrenica and Zepa towards free territory of Tuzla and Kladanj, nothing was done to help them, to come to their assistance; that is to say, what was done was negligible, insufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I apologise once again for interrupting, but could you explain to us what the strategic interest was or military -- particularly military interest as regards Srebrenica for the Bosnia-Herzegovina army forces and the VRS army forces? What were their strategic interests?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: The strategic goal of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was defined by the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the platform taken by the presidency on wartime circumstances which was enacted on the 1st of June, 1992, therefore, a free Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state of equal peoples of the Bosniaks, Bosnian Serbs, Bosnian Croats, and all other peoples living in that territory. And of course, our strategic goal was to have a free, liberated Podrinje. The strategic goal of the Bosnian Serbs was defined by their own decision, a decision taken by their assembly, which was to have ethnically cleansed the valley of the Drina, and as it says, to do away with the Drina as being a centuries-old border between Serb states, which means that our two sides were on opposite sides in the Drina valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, to move on to the attack on Srebrenica, do you have an idea when the Bosniak authorities, civilian or military, learnt of the attack on the Srebrenica enclave by the Serb forces, and in particular, when were they informed of the transfer of the population, the capture, and then the execution of members of the column and so on and so forth? When did they learn of this? And the BH army forces, did they have military materiel and manpower to prevent the attack or to launch a counter-attack? Could you develop your ideas along those lines, please. May we have your opinion on that area? What is your information on that subject?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: In the Dani magazine published in 1998 as a special edition, Dani magazine, under the title of "How They Sold Out Srebrenica and Retained Power," this was an article written by Mr. Hecimovic, a journalist, he quotes a series of testimonies from the meeting of the SDA Main Board in Zenica, and he quotes the speech on that occasion made by the then-commander Rasim Delic, who, in his 20-minute-long presentation, devoted several minutes to the Srebrenica situation. The meeting of the Main Board of the SDA party in Zenica, and the fall of the enclave of Srebrenica, occurred on the same day; it coincided. He just informed them Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at the meeting that NATO planes, two planes were active over Srebrenica, and says nothing more on the subject. Hecimovic at that time was a journalist and he was a close collaborator of the prime minister, Mr. Haris Silajdzic, prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, therefore, he was in a position to know at firsthand what was happening there. I later learnt that the command of the 2nd Corps and the General Staff knew when the operation on Srebrenica started, but from a series of testimonies, the people who were in Srebrenica, both from military and political structures, we can clearly see that they asked for help, both of the command of the 2nd Corps and the command of the General Staff and President Izetbegovic, but that they did not receive that assistance. To answer your question whether they had the power and materiel to help, to come to the help of Srebrenica, I think that they did. First of all, what was needed was, before the Sarajevo operation, to ensure Srebrenica and Zepa, to protect it, and they had enough manpower and enough materiel to do so - that is my opinion - and not to unleash the Sarajevo operation and to leave Srebrenica and Zepa to fend for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General. Perhaps we could now move on more specifically to the column, the issue of the column. In general terms, what information do you dispose of with respect to the column, the formation of the column, the evolution of the column, and everything else with respect to the column, how it was pierced?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: From what I learnt talking to people who were in the enclave, that is to say, in Srebrenica, but also from the discussions I had with members of the General Staff, I learnt that, in fact, the General Staff and the presidency did not have any information as to the direction taken by the column from Srebrenica. They reported back once but did not communicate after that, so that in practical terms, the first information as to the direction of the column, whether it was moving towards Zepa or Kladanj or Tuzla, reached them only when the first parts of the column began to appear along the Tuzla axis, which means that along that route of horror from Srebrenica to Tuzla, they were not assisted in any way. No aid was provided. And as to the movement of the column itself and the terrible sufferings that they went through, there are many testimonies to this ordeal, and they can be ranked amongst the greatest horror experiences imaginable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, do you have any information as to the time when the Bosnian authorities learnt about the capture of one portion of the column and how those authorities actually learnt about the executions and the disappearance of a number of members of that column? When was it that they learnt about it, and how did they learn about it?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: My knowledge about that is based on written documents, and I must admit that I'm not quite sure as to their reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you one more question about the column. Was there an operation conducted from the direction of Tuzla at the same time? For example, did Naser Oric receive an order not to go and search for the column? What was the view of the situation from the perspective of Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: What Naser Oric told me about it, and what his associates who were in the area of Tuzla at the time told me, was that he had requested help, both from the General Staff and the Corps Command, that a passage be opened through which the column could pass. But he also complained about the lack of understanding on their part. He told me that finally, in the end, he had managed to gather a group of people on his own - that group of people was not very large, maybe 50 members only - and that he had attempted to pierce the corridor at one spot and open up a passage which should have been used by the column. When he spoke about that, he and his associates, they were very angry and resigned. So my knowledge about that particular aspect of the situation is based on their experience and not on my personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. I think that we already have enough information at this point, so we could perhaps have a break now. After the break, the parties will have some questions for you, and after their questions, the Judges might also have questions for you. Let me ask the usher to accompany General Halilovic out of the courtroom first. We will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Harmon, 50 minutes, approximately, for your questions. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Good morning, General. Mr. President, we have no questions of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Petrusic. Examined by Mr. Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General. My name is Nenad Petrusic and I am defending General Krstic in this case. I have a few questions for you. Let me begin with the end of your narrative. You told us that it was through the conversations with Mr. Oric that you learnt about the fact that there was no communication, no contact, and that it was because of that that no adequate assistance was ever provided to the units which had attempted to break through from the direction of Srebrenica towards Kladanj. General, I would like to know whether you know Sead Delic, General Delic.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I know General Delic by sight. We never had an opportunity to talk, so I only know him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a General with the BH army, was he not, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, General Sead Delic, I assume because he was an active, high-ranking officer of the BH army in 1995 - unlike yourself who at the time was no longer in any command function with the BH army, if I understand you correctly - was informed about the events which were taking place at the front line. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I don't know whether it was on purpose or accidentally, but you have reversed the things in your allegation just now. I stated that I had talks with some members of the General Staff of the BH army, and that in those conversations, they had told me that there had been no contact with them and that they were not informed of the direction which the column had taken; whereas Naser Oric told me that he had requested assistance from the General Staff and the commander of the 2nd Corps, General Delic, that is, that they give him the units with which he could open up a passage for the column to pull out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would you agree with me that General Delic was informed about the events taking place at the front line in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: From what I know - and the basis of my knowledge are various sources, including magazines and a number of statements - one can conclude that General Sead Delic had been informed about the events taking place at the front line up until the moment when the column decided to attempt a breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, General Sead Delic in an interview which he gave to the Dani magazine on the 17th of March, 2000, in response to a question put to him by a journalist to the effect that there were two rumours circulating amongst the population from Srebrenica, first of all, that after the fall of Srebrenica, Oric broke through the lines of Serb forces with a number of volunteers, and second story, that he had refused, cowardly so, to attempt that breakthrough, General Sead Delic answered to that question "neither of both." He went on to state that it was on the 13th of July that Oric received an order to take a number of soldiers and officers and launch combat activities in the area of Medzedza. General, you would agree with me that Medzedza is in the area of the breakthrough line of the 28th Division in the direction of Kladanj. Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: You must admit that from General Delic's statement --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General, excuse me for a second. Would you please answer my question, that is, is Medzedza in the area of the breakthrough of the 28th Division in the direction of Kladanj? Could you simply answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the first part of your question is far more important, but I will answer the second part as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a copy of the article that's being referred to by my colleague and about which questions are being directed to General Halilovic. Perhaps General Halilovic could be shown the article that is the subject of these questions, and he would be better prepared to answer the questions of my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we should perhaps wait for the question and then the answer of the witness. General Halilovic is probably familiar with the article. If he needs it, on the other hand, I think that Mr. Petrusic can provide him with a copy of the article, if the General wishes to have a copy in front of him. But thanks for your intervention, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Petrusic, could you perhaps ask your question once again, and if necessary, could you give the article to the General, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would you first of all answer my question, that is, is Medzedza in the area of the breakthrough of the 28th Division which was moving from the direction of Srebrenica towards Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I will answer your question; however, with your permission, I should like to comment on the statement which was given by Mr. Sead Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Because you phrased it that way, I think that that portion of your question was more important than the exact location of Medzedza. The question to which Sead Delic responded is far more significant, and your question is a formal one and meaningless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, it is not up to you to assess the significance of the question. Thank you very much for your opinion, but I insist on my question. Can I please have your answer.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: General Sead Delic merely confirmed what Naser Oric had said, that a number of soldiers and officers had received an order to that effect, and you must admit that such an order cannot be carried out by that number of soldiers and officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you stated that there was no knowledge about the direction which the column had taken in its breakthrough and that nobody knew where they would attempt a breakthrough. Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Counsel, I told you what I had heard from the members of the General Staff who held very high positions within the Main Staff of the BH army. They claim that that was correct, that they were not informed of the direction of the moving of the 28th Division up until the moment when they actually appeared in the free territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Sead Delic goes on in his interview and he states as follows: "They left in the afternoon hours and then they attempted to establish the contact with the elements of the 28th Division which moved in the direction of Tuzla. A soldier had passed through the area two days ago and came to Kalesija, in the area of the Kalesija, and we concluded from his story that that was also the possible line of their movement." Does that mean, General, that the command of the 2nd Corps was familiar with the direction of the breakthrough of the 28th Division, if, as early as the 11th of July, they had the particular piece of information at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: If you should read the answer of General Delic once again, and carefully so, you will realise that he too says at one point that it was their conclusion that it would be possible, and so on and so forth. So he himself was not sure as to the direction of the movement of the column. It was merely his assumption, and he said that it would be possible. So from his answer, we can see that the statements given by the people who held very high positions within the General Staff of the BH army are confirmed, that is, that it was merely their assumption but that they were not sure as to the exact direction of the movement of the column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Sead Delic goes on and states in his interview that: "The front line, which was two kilometres long, was pierced by the units from Srebrenik [as interpreted]. The 11th Brigade and the 241st and the 242st and 43rd Brigades also took part in the breakthrough. Those units were in the strength of a company. I personally went, together with Senahid Hodzic, the commander of the 281st Brigade there. He was the only commanding officer at the time who managed to reach the area of Baljkovica and crossed over to the other side." Does this mean, General, this statement of General Sead Delic, that the units of the 2nd Corps had participated in the breakthrough and the pull-out of the troops of the 28th Division from encirclement?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: General Delic himself confirms the fact that from these three brigades you have just mentioned, only portions in the strength of a company were engaged; that is, only certain elements were there. So this statement is the confirmation of what Oric told me, that is, that those units were not very strong ones and that without appropriate artillery and other support were unable to conduct such a complex assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, immediately prior to the attack on Srebrenica, and also throughout 1995, that is, not earlier than 1995, were any diversionary and terrorist units, sabotage units, organised in that area, according to your knowledge? Were they active in that area?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the structure and the organisation of our units, I think that you are quite knowledgeable about that. You know that there are sabotage units within each brigade, so there were such units, sabotage units, throughout BH army brigades. There is nothing in dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your knowledge, General, that those sabotage and terrorist units made incursions into the territory which was outside the enclave of Srebrenica, that is, outside the borders of the safe area?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: As regards one order which I had access to -- that is, I have already spoken about one such order that I had at my disposal. As to whether there were several such orders, I don't have any information about that. But I do know that throughout that period of time, that is, from the 8th of May, 1993, up until the fall of the enclave, practically speaking, that is, until the month of July, 1995, there were several attacks by paramilitary forces of Bosnian Serbs. You can learn about that if you read the special report of the Secretary-General of the United Nations, which I hope you have. If you do not, I can provide it to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about the attacks of paramilitary forces. Are you referring to the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I've been using the term which was used in United Nations resolutions, Resolution 819 and several other relevant resolutions issued by the Security Council of the United Nations. They used the term, and I think it would be only fair enough for me to use that particular term and not any other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, it is not my intention to enter into a debate with you, but do you happen to know what term was used in the report of the Secretary-General of the United Nations, if we are speaking about -- since you have mentioned international organisations yourself?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: All institutions belonging to the International Community refer to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was some mistakes made from time to time, but that is not important. What is important was the fact that it was a legal army of the internationally recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only wanted to say that in the report made by Kofi Annan, the "VRS" term is also used, the army of Bosnian Serbs, that is.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can always check that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, as a high-ranking officer of the former JNA and the BH army, do you think that any conduct of terrorist activities in spring of that year, that is, terrorist activities from the enclave, from the protected area and into the Serbian-held territory, against Serbian-held positions, was something that could trigger offensive action by the VRS towards the area of the enclave, towards the safe area?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: If there had indeed been terrorist activities from the enclave, I consider it to be a mistake. Would you please allow me to finish the question with one more sentence. I think this is an essential issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence is happy with the answer of the witness, but it is really up to you whether you're going to let him finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Halilovic, there will be questions of the Judges later on. For the time being, you are here to answer questions put to you by the Defence counsel, and it is really up to them to decide what questions they want to ask of you. You now have to answer, if you want to do so, the question that is put to you by the Defence counsel, and later on, as I have indicated, there will be questions of the Judges. Mr. Petrusic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you are one of the signatories of the agreement on demilitarisation. I should like to know -- and of course, you are also familiar with the rights and duties which during that period of time you yourself and, later on, those who succeeded you on your functions, members of the BH army, had to respect. Does that agreement envisage any sanctions for either of the parties in case of non-compliance with the agreement?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: While I was still a member of the BH army, the agreement was complied with in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have any knowledge whether in the spring and summer of 1995 the said agreement was honoured and complied with?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Under the assumption that one single terrorist activity had been conducted, then one was supposed to request that the Security Council of the United Nations to withdraw the agreement concerning the safe area, and one had to publicly state that the agreement was no longer binding and not launch an attack which had horrible consequences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in those years, did you happen to know, and do you still know, a prominent politician in Bosnia and Herzegovina, an individual by the name of Rusomir Mahmut Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic, is his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. At the time, he was vice-president of -- vice-premier, and now he's a researcher. He's a president of a scientific association.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he an influential politician in those years?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: At the time he was a vice-prime minister, and he had adequate influence, depending on his function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, General, together with Naser Oric, have an opportunity to talk to Mr. Mahmut Cehajic after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We talked in the spring of 1996, and that conversation was published by Oslobodenje Daily in the summer of 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the conversation which was published by Oslobodenje Daily in four segments, in four installments in August 1996, was never authorised. You never denied it, you never denied what you said during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: There was no need to deny anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that conversation that the two of you had, Mr. Oric states, I quote, "At any time of day and night from the very beginning of the war up until June 1993, until the arrival of Delic, I had contact with commander Sefer through radio line, radio communication. He was the only person who knew exactly what was happening. And when the order on demilitarisation of the town itself was issued, the commander explained to me that we should hand over only non-functional and faulty weaponry, the ones that we could not hide, heavy weapons, which is what I did. We remained deployed along the lines and the weapons were still with us." Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: The agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa envisaged the demilitarisation of the urban areas of those two towns and the pull-out of all personnel from the area. After I returned from the airport on the 9th of May, I issued an order specifying that not a single piece of weaponry and equipment should be handed over because we had some very bad experience to that effect, that is, with very slow and inefficient decisions by the International Community. So yes, you're quite correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Mr. Oric stated on that occasion that all of the weaponry which had been handed over was not usable and was faulty, and that all other weapons, the ones that were functional, were still kept?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: You just stated that Naser Oric had said that I was familiar with everything that was happening, and that is quite true, but to the effect it was possible to learn about the situation through radio communication. According to a report sent to me by Naser Oric, old and dysfunctional weapons had been handed over, and those who -- those that could still be used were kept, and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that conversation, General, you say that you had ordered that only the useless weapons should be surrendered. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: According to the agreement on the demilitarisation of the urban area of Srebrenica and Zepa, we were not obliged to surrender anything. But it is true that I had ordered, if they had to surrender something, that they should surrender what was faulty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in your book "Failed Strategy" published in 1998, you also say, I quote, "I returned to headquarters and issued an order to Srebrenica and Zepa that not a single functional piece of weaponry should be handed over or a single usable bullet. After that, I went to see Izetbegovic and was given congratulations for success." General, you're talking about the urban area; however, clearly your order did not apply to the urban area regarding the surrender of equipment and weaponry.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: You must distinguish between the safe area and the demilitarised zone. According to the agreement, the demilitarised zone covers the urban area of Srebrenica and Zepa and what can be seen from the town itself, and within that zone, no armed personnel or military equipment were permitted. Therefore, my order was to pull out from that area, pursuant to the agreement, all armed personnel and military equipment and, of course, to preserve and retain those weapons that we could use should we launch an attack, if that should prove necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you are familiar with the decision of the United Nations which had a no-fly zone envisaged.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pursuant to that decision, were military and civilian aircraft prohibited from flying over from one territory to another, that is, specifically from Tuzla to Srebrenica and Zepa? My question is, were flights prohibited?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, flights were prohibited for military purposes, but units of the air force of the Yugoslav army - I'm referring to airplanes and helicopters - were used during the attack on Srebrenica and Zepa from January 1993 until May 1993. And testifying to this was General Morillon - I think he wrote about it - who personally witnessed the takeoff of aircraft from the Ponikve strip. It was medical material that was transported more than combat equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but such flights were in violation of the United Nations' decision, whether it was partial violation or total, but in any event, it was in violation of that agreement. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously not, because the opposite side -- I don't want to have a dispute with you regarding the term, used airplanes and helicopters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm not asking you about the opposing side. I'm talking to you about aircraft of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or aircraft of the civilian authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina without the approval of the United Nations. Was that a violation of the resolution?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Partially yes, because we were transported -- transporting food and medicaments mostly, but partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a violation if ammunition were transported by means of those aircraft and helicopters? Will you answer that question, please, with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that we were under an embargo and our hands were tied, I think not. Morally, no; legally, one could discuss it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Naser Oric, General, says in this newspaper Oslobodenje, an interview that you attended as did Mr. Mahmut Cehajic, that Sefer sent six helicopters with ammunition. Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: It is not correct. It is correct that I sent eight helicopters with ammunition, and if I could have, I would have sent 180.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you were violating the provisions of the United Nations resolution.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: The legal norms of the United Nations also guarantee the right to defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in view of the fact that you sent eight helicopters within a short span of time to Srebrenica, was there sufficient weaponry and ammunition in Srebrenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. If there had been, the combat operations would have evolved differently in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain the need for weapons and ammunitions of the 28th Division in Srebrenica, if UNPROFOR forces were present and constituted a buffer zone between the Serb and Muslim sides?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: So as not to misinform the Trial Chamber, I'm talking about eight helicopters in the period from January to May 1993. The UN proclaimed the safe areas, but they never had sufficient forces and resources to secure them. Sarajevo too was a safe area, and 1.600 people were killed and more than a million shells fell on the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, on that occasion, did Naser Oric tell you upon whose orders, in the last decade, of April 1995 he and a number of other senior officers left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: He told me that he left Srebrenica upon orders of the Chief of Staff of the General Staff. In those days, I think it was Enver Hadzihasanovic. And I think he will be here in the courtroom after me, and then you can ask him that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you have any knowledge, during the time of the attack on Srebrenica, how the 28th Division was structured? Let me withdraw that question. Perhaps General Hadzihasanovic can tell us more about that.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I could tell you, but I think he is more qualified to give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, excuse me, but do I have also 50 minutes, so that I can organise myself within that time frame? In the event that I may take a few minutes longer, will you please caution me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you should overstep 50 minutes, there will be no punishment for you. If you do need more time, please do so. We'll allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much, I hope. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you mentioned the 15th of June as the day when the deblocking or the offensive operations to deblock Sarajevo was embarked upon?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: In those days, there were a large number of orders for sabotage operations from the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a high-ranking officer of the former Yugoslav People's Army and of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who is familiar with the doctrine and strategy and rules, that that was intended to draw away forces from one battlefront to another [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: If there were any such orders, then you should have used them to ask the United Nations to nullify the resolution on safe areas. I think that would have been the proper course for you to take, rather than doing what you did in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have any knowledge that your army or political leadership or Supreme Command asked for the abolition of the safe areas, in view of what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge whether any such requests were made. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have any knowledge regarding the fact that the 28th Division had a plan of attack on members of UNPROFOR and their equipment? Of course, that was a period when you were not the commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the period of 1994, 1995.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I read about some such plans in the press, but the testimony of Enver Hadzihasanovic will be more appropriate in that context, as he was Chief of Staff at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I will put a question to you, a hypothetical. If one party to a conflict, regardless of which party that may be, attacks another and violates certain norms and agreements, is it the legitimate right of the other party to retaliate and respond? General, this is a hypothetical question and it doesn't apply to Srebrenica or any other specific situation. General, I'm -- it was the side that you are representing that violated the provisions of the assigned agreement. General, this is a hypothetical question and you obviously don't want to answer it.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, the opposite side should observe the norms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. If you overlap, it is simply not possible to translate what you are saying. You have to speak one after the other, with pauses in between. And General Halilovic, answer, please, Mr. Petrusic's question. Please continue, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm waiting for your answer.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me a question without allowing me to answer it. So hypothetically -- your question is a hypothetical one, and yet you know that the units of the opposite side violated the agreement all the time. And if units of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina acted in violation of the agreement, then the lawful procedure would be to ask for the abolition of the decision of a safe area, to withdraw your signature from the agreements, and then you would have the legitimate right to respond; until then, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did the other side too in this case -- I withdraw that question. General, do you know Hakija Meholjic? Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I met him in 1999 or 2000 perhaps, after having read some of his statements in the press.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, he was chief of police in Srebrenica in 1995, or rather, in the period of the safe area until the end of the war. Is that so, for the record?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the technical booth to play a short video film of some 10 minutes. It is a video film made by Dutch television, after which I will have a few Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. questions for the General, General Halilovic. My colleague is correcting me. It will take 12 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we need an interpreter to interpret from the Dutch into English; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. In the break I spoke to the technical booth, and they have provided a translation so that the Chamber and the parties can follow the film, and not just the witness and the Defence, as there is a translation in the Serbian and in Dutch.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't have anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Petrusic, that we only have a Dutch version, so we need interpretation. Do you have a B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean a transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The video is in three languages, depending on who is speaking. When they're speaking Bosnian, representatives of the Bosnian authorities, they use their own language, of course; when a journalist is speaking, who is filming, he speaks his language, which is Dutch; and then in a couple of shots we have the English subtitles too. So I think we can look at the video and then, through the questions, clear up anything that may not be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us try, but I see that General Halilovic has something to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood Mr. Petrusic correctly, the event has to do with 1995, and I think General Hadzihasanovic's opinion would be more relevant, in view of his position in the army at the time, and I fear that we may be wasting time for no purpose, in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will not be wasting time, because there is a statement by General Hadzihasanovic on that tape - no, I'm sorry - General Halilovic on the video, so I do consider it relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let us see the video clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no sound, to the technical booth. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, from the little bit I've seen - not heard, of course, but seen - it appears there's Dutch subtitles, and the Prosecution bench doesn't have a Dutch speaker or a B/C/S speaker, and so we are unable to understand, essentially, what may be a significant part of this film. If this film has been available for a considerable period of time, it seems to me the transcripts should have been prepared on this film and made available to us; otherwise we're sitting here like people in a movie theatre watching a foreign film, and it is meaningless to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was proceeding from the principle that we did need an interpreter from the Dutch into another language, but if the footage was in B/C/S, it would be possible to translate, I thought. But there is an interpreter, Thomas Henquet, I understand, to do the translation. Do you have a microphone, Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Mr. President, it's a technical matter. The video is in three languages, Dutch, English, and B/C/S. Mr. Henquet reviewed the tape yesterday, and if the Chamber so wishes, he is ready to interpret it simultaneously, though he is not a professional interpreter. He's ready to interpret the parts that are in Dutch. There is no transcript today of that footage. That cassette was tendered by the Defence. It was shown by Dutch television for the first time in March 2001, and it was tendered to registry on the 21st of March this year, so there was no time to prepare a transcript in the three official languages of the Tribunal because speakers use different languages in the footage. If you so wish and if necessary, Mr. Henquet may take a solemn declaration. He can go to the English booth, and with the assistance of the technical booth, you would be able to view this video and thus obtain a French or English or B/C/S version as you may require. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, what do you say to this suggestion? Is it acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I'm addressing myself to Mr. Thomas Henquet. Could you please get up. Stand up, please. Do you take upon yourself to accomplish this task with loyalty, independence, and impartiality, and in full respect of your duty to preserve confidentiality?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENQUET
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Henquet has answered with a "yes, I do." I'm saying this because he didn't have a microphone so the interpreters were unable to interpret. Mr. Thomas, please go to the English booth. [In English] Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, okay. So from the technical booth, are you ready? Okay, let's go.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Alija was telling us about the offer of Clinton. Chetniks would take Srebrenica and kill 5.000 Muslims, and there will be a military intervention. What did we think about that? We rejected that. We didn't think it was normal to have 5.000 people being killed." I can't hear the commentary, I'm sorry. I cannot hear the Dutch comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we need to start from the beginning. The English booth tells us that they cannot hear the sound of the commentary in Dutch, so they can't translate it. I think perhaps it would be better to have a break. We've been working for about an hour and ten minutes, so maybe we should have a break and then the technical booth can prepare everything so that things run smoothly. So General Halilovic, we're going to have a short break. Mr. Usher, a break. Twenty-minute break. --- Break taken at 11.59 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the interpreters and the technical booth have invested a great deal of effort to adapt themselves to a situation which is not usual, and therefore for people to be able to follow the discussion, I am going to ask Mr. Olivier Fourmy to give us the instructions that he has received from the technicians themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In effect, when we are showing a videotape, the normal thing is to have a transcript of what is on the tape so that the interpreters are able to interpret precisely. In this extraordinary situation, and we should like to apologise on behalf of the registry, people wishing to listen in the B/C/S language should listen to it on channel 6 and will have to focus their attention on the headsets because it is technically not possible to delete the volume of the cassette in the public gallery, so at times there will be an overlapping of voices. You will hear the voice of the speaker in the B/C/S, and as the interpretation will be done from the English, there might be some overlapping. But as to what is said on the tape, I suggest that you focus on the interpretation coming from the booths. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean, Mr. Fourmy, that English will still be on channel 4 and French will continue to be on channel 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We shall try. Let us have the videotape played now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "A meeting with American president Clinton, Alija was telling us about the offer of Clinton. Chetniks would take Srebrenica and kill 5.000 Muslims, and then there will be a military intervention, and what did we think about that? And we rejected that. We didn't think it was normal that 5.000 people would be slaughtered. That the American president would have suggested that Serbs would enter Srebrenica and to kill Muslims in order to justify an intervention would be too absurd, but from the UN research, it now seems that this is not too awkward. Some surviving members of the Srebrenica delegation have stated that President Izetbegovic also told them that he had learned that a NATO intervention in Bosnia-Herzegovina was possible but could only occur if the Serbs which would break into Srebrenica are killing at least 5.000 of its people. President Izetbegovic was heard by UN investigators and denies having made those statements, but he admits having accepted an opinion on the exchange of territories. We talked about an exchange and the exchange of Srebrenica for other territories. UN report: The delegation opposed the idea and the subject was not discussed further. In negotiations we will demand that the maps will be corrected in the Bosnian parliament, that the Bosnian Republic will get Muslim territory along the Drina. The delegation is -- imposed secrecy. The exchange of territories is not -- it was not abolished. We agreed to meet the next day. But after our meeting with Izetbegovic, people started to be bribed. People were taken everywhere. Men came that I didn't know and they made propositions. I've seen those men, but never again afterwards. They spoke individually with us or in groups, sitting at a table. I was sitting at a table together with Mehovic, and they asked us what we thought about Srebrenica for Vogosca, exchanging for Srebrenica for Vogosca, and Zepa for Ilijas.
