In case I would not accept the exchange, I could be liquidated, so I returned with the delegation to Srebrenica. General Halilovic was aware of the meeting between Izetbegovic and the delegation. According to him, the president spoke also with other representatives of Srebrenica. Izetbegovic offered to exchange Srebrenica for Zepa, for neighbourhoods in Sarajevo, Vogosca, Ilijas and Ilidza. We rejected that. Only half a year after Srebrenica was proclaimed a safe area, it is the Muslim government that discusses the destiny of the Muslim population in Srebrenica. Did Sarajevo sacrifice Srebrenica in 1993? Answer: I think so, yes. From these facts emerges that maintaining Srebrenica was not a prime objective of the Muslim government. Half a year later, the first Dutch blue helmets arrive at Srebrenica. In spite of limited support in Dutch parliament, they are tasked to defend the enclave. This is the Dutch minister for the Defence: We know that you are in a very difficult position here and that you have to do a very difficult job here, and you're very important for the future of these people. Lieutenant Colonel Broskij, acting commander of DutchBat, is convinced the Dutch government did not know about the -- but I did give up Srebrenica. I cannot imagine that the Dutch government was aware of those plans, that is, to give up Srebrenica, that those negotiations were going on. I'm really not -- I'm sure that we didn't know that. Interview of the Dutch Defence Ministry for [unintelligible] Srebrenica. You see a lot of people who are really waiting for a future that they don't know -- they don't know what the future will bring, and you see that they realise that they are incredibly dependent upon DutchBat and that DutchBat is really a life insurance for them. DutchBat is a life insurance for them. The question is: Would the Dutch government have sent DutchBat if they had known that the Muslims were considering the secret proposal and maybe have accepted that? Broskij, acting commander of DutchBat, says that this would have been decisive. This is Broskij, the acting commander: Well, the situation would have been different for the Dutch government in that case. I'm certain of that. And perhaps -- Question: -- Answer: We would not have been sent in that case. Early 1995, after a year of relative quiet, tensions increase in the enclave. February, a year and a half after the issue of exchange of territory was discussed -- they're talking about a discussion with Naser Oric. The one general refuses to take Oric with him. Early April 1995 Oric would have managed to speak to Izetbegovic and to discuss his presumptions. In the General Staff, according to this man, there was a meeting between Oric and Izetbegovic. I heard from Naser that those two were together in one room during that night. Naser told me that himself. Everything indicates that Oric's fears were confirmed. Oric is back from Kakanj, but then he leaves for good from the enclave and he orders the deputy commander to come with him. After that, he told me, I don't know the exact number, but he sent about 20 officers away, known fighters who participated in heavy fighting. They were trusted by the soldiers and by the people. Each of them could easily gather a hundred people with them that were willing and able to die, able to die. He sent them away to study, to follow an education. Sources confirm that Oric left on his own initiative. The soldiers spoke to Oric just before Oric left. He said he would come back. He said that he would come back and arrange something for our enclave. The man who had been in the centre of attention for four years left in silence. DutchBat and the UN left -- knew that Oric has been in safety for three months only after the fall of Srebrenica. Is this his biggest secret? Answer: Probably. His secret and Izetbegovic's secret. Dutch deputy commander: He was a very strong leader. The people, he really -- he was a very strong force behind his brigades, at the moment such a commander, at least, and case is complete. People panicked, especially women, children, and elderly, so the weaker groups. And the little bit of army that was left started to panic. We saw that there was no more leadership, and we had obviously been abandoned. Around Srebrenica, Serbian troops started to pull together and they started to regroup, restructure. June 1995, everything indicates that the Serbs are preparing their final offensive. DutchBat is preparing -- it's preparing itself. Then something strange happened. Muslim soldiers leave the enclave and plunder the village of Visnjica just behind the defence line. The order came from Sarajevo to change the pressure on the front. In the meeting, I resisted. This could not happen because this would cause problems. The village was very unimportant. Still the order was given, and the guys in Srebrenica followed the order. Why, for goodness' sake? Houses were burned. The attack was led by one of Oric's former allies, former associates. 11th of July, 1995, Serbs take the enclave. The Muslims are separated. Women and children are bused to safety. The men stay behind. The remaining army, the remaining part of the army flees through the woods to Tuzla. According to official estimates, 7.000 men were killed with premeditation by Serbs. No one could prevent the fall of the enclave; DutchBat, the UN, but also the Muslim -- the DutchBat Brigade, all the Muslim forces. Everybody remained passive. Shortly after Srebrenica, the enclave Zepa fell into Serb hands. Meanwhile, around Sarajevo, another battle is going on. Suddenly five Serb Ops fall into Muslim hands, therewith, the siege of Sarajevo will soon end. This is the conclusion. I still respect for Dudakovic and the 5th Army Corps, but in three days, take five cities. Where was he all that time? I've been in war myself, and I know what war is. Gorazde was awaiting the same fate as us. Serbs killed more people than was planned. Definitely Gorazde, otherwise Gorazde would have been the same fate as Srebrenica. The International Community needed the genocide to stop this war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, sir, you will agree that the man on this video clip speaking about the alleged agreement of Alija Izetbegovic on the liquidation of 5.000 Muslims was Hakija Meholjic; am I right in saying that? For the record, you assert that it was Hakija Meholjic?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was Hakija Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, sir, Hakija Meholjic speaks about meetings that were held in Sarajevo at the Holiday Inn there or at some other location, and you in your book, "The Aborted Strategy," you yourself speak about that, and I quote from page 131 of your book. You say as follows: "I was twice present when Izetbegovic in Sarajevo in the early spring of 1993 offered the representatives of Srebrenica and Zepa that this kind of exchange be conducted, be made to: Srebrenica and Zepa for the environs of Sarajevo, Vogosca, and Ilijas. The proposal after the consultation with the people and with the fighters was resolutely rejected." Was that so, General; that is to say, were you, in fact, present?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I was present in March and May 1993 when Izetbegovic talked to Murat Efendic and Dr. Becim Hendic [phoen] and some other people from Srebrenica and Zepa, and when they were offered this exchange, Srebrenica and Zepa for the Sarajevo environs, and Mr. Hakija Meholjic spoke about the talk with Izetbegovic and what they discussed about Srebrenica and Zepa, that was in September 1993. So they are two different meetings, in fact. And when Izetbegovic talked to Meholjic and that delegation, and the delegation which came from Srebrenica, in fact, I was not present on that particular occasion, but I did attend the talks in the May, March period, March to May period, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the second meeting, September 1993? You were informed about that through the media; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: The September meeting, 1993, Hakija Meholjic I think spoke to the journal Dani or Slobodna Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hakija Meholjic was a policeman, or rather, the chief of police in Srebrenica, and he brings -- makes a connection between the leaving of Srebrenica by the commander of the 8th Operative Group, Naser Oric, and his 20-odd men, subordinate commanding officers. So he brings that fact, he ties it in with the agreement which was offered in 1993 on two occasions to the Muslim side. Do you, from what he said, have the same conclusion to make?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I have already given my answer to your question at the beginning of my testimony. I said that it was a tactical mistake that the leadership, political and military, of Bosnia-Herzegovina made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, sir, we are nearing the end, and as we do so, I should like to quote a portion of your book, page 132, and I open quotations: "The operation to deblock Sarajevo began on the 15th of June, 1995, and the Chetniks entered Srebrenica on the 11th of July, 1995, with three tanks, two transporters, APCs, and about 200 Chetniks. While the Chetniks were entering Srebrenica, in Zenica the main council was meeting at the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA party, and the security -- there was more security there than was the occupation army in Srebrenica." According to your knowledge, General, that is to say, was your information directed towards this number of soldiers and the equipment they had at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: What I say in my book, "A Sly Strategy," I based on my talk with David Rhode and his book, "The End of the Game," published in 1997; and also on a special edition of the Dani journal entitled "How They Gave Over Srebrenica"; and also I base this on my discussions with other people, talks to other people who were present in Srebrenica and Zenica, and I had these talks in 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, General, I'm going to quote one more sentence, page 134 of your book, and I quote: "According to an interview with Holbrooke, Izetbegovic in January 1995 was ready to hand over Srebrenica to the Serbs in the context of a broader solution of the peace question and in order to retain Sarajevo intact. He said that they were not his, and he did not care about that. Mark Dunner [phoen] recorded Holbrooke's statement on that occasion." When you say he did not care about that, that they were not his people, do you mean "he" being Alija Izetbegovic? Is that the "he" you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: It is not I who say that. I was quoting Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Dunner, so I was just quoting what they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we conclude that this refers to the then president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Here it states precisely that it refers to Mr. Izetbegovic, and there is no need for us to deduce anything. It says so clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the Defence has no further questions for you. We have completed our examination. Thank you for testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that completes the examination by the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. I think that the time has come for our lunch break, that this would be an opportune moment to adjourn. It is customary to have two breaks during the morning session, but we have allowed more time for the technical difficulties that we had. So could we now take a 45-minute break and reconvene after that. But before we adjourn, I'm going to ask the usher to escort General Halilovic out of the courtroom. We adjourn for 45 minutes. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.56 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Judge Fouad Riad, I should like to thank Mr. Thomas Henquet for his very good work and for having assisted us in the interpretation. And having said that, I give the floor, without further ado, to Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General Halilovic, good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps you could be in a position to throw some more light on the information you gave us in your testimony and in your paper. My first questions are related to the column in the woods. If you can answer me, I'll be very grateful. What urged the civilians to go into a column into the woods?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't answer that question, because at that time I was only able to follow the situation there via the media, so I cannot say with any certainty what that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What constituted their fears? You know you cannot tell about that.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Having the experience with Serbian paramilitary formations from the start of war up until July 1995, the deduction is very simple. We can conclude very simply what it was all about and why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the experience thus far, and knowing of the methods of warfare that existed in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and how they fought the Bosnian civilians in the first place, and all the experience gained and the fears that they had, we can conclude why they were afraid and why they took that particular road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You want to say they were afraid for their lives?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The column was, according to your report, at least the majority, composed of civilians. Did I understand rightly? What was the percentage of fighters or of military people in the column, if you know about it?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly what the percentage of military people was compared to the civilians in the column, but after the breakthrough from the encirclement -- from the enclave, rather, several days later I saw a review of the 28th Division in Tuzla, and there were about 3.000 soldiers, 3.000 fighters amongst them, and the information media claimed that they came from the enclave to Tuzla together with the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And have you an idea how strongly they were armed in the column?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who were in the column together with the civilians were armed with light infantry weapons. That was shown during the review and ceremony held in Tuzla seven or eight days later, after they had broken through, after they had exited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And were they in a position to fight, to fight back?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Their position was a highly precarious one, and according to what I learnt, once again from the information media, they had to walk for a very long time and were very tired. They were exhausted, and a large number did not reach Tuzla at all, so that they were not in a position to defend themselves, to fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned in your report that the Serbian forces launched an artillery against the column. What justified this use of artillery against the column?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: For that kind of use of the artillery, there is no justification or reason, either human or military. The object was to destroy as many military-abled people as possible, or rather, as many Bosniaks as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was not a military, a military target?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, they were non-selective in their targeting, so it was immaterial whether they were military or civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was this a peaceful -- these military people in the column able to contact the Muslim forces outside the forest? Did they have means of communication?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: The conclusion that I arrived at is that they did not have the possibility of contacting anyone, and that the -- nor did the Corps Command or the General Staff know which way they were heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You spoke about the indiscriminate shooting. What about the executions? Because you mentioned that there was a real hunt after the men in the second part of the column, and upon surrendering or being captured, they were also killed at various sites. Now, was this killing also indiscriminate, or was it directed towards certain fighters or that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, based on the information media and the testimony of those who escaped from the enclave, everybody was killed at random, indiscriminately, regardless of whether they were fighters or civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You spoke about people escaping from the enclave. Did you, by any chance, have any contact with some of those who survived to tell you what happened?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have contact with some of the people who had left the enclave, and their stories, the stories they tell, are far worse than the blackest of horror movies that the human mind has been able to conjure up so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did they tell you that among those that shot them or executed them were soldiers of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: When they spoke, they said that the Chetniks shot at them. They didn't speak about -- they couldn't know what the units were, what military formations they were members of, but it is to be assumed that the majority of those who did that were from the Drina Corps. That is what one can conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could they know that the people who shot at them were military people or were bands of gangsters?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: According to their testimonies, they were army members, members of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, going to the entry of Srebrenica, you -- I could gather from what you said, from your report and from what was said also in the -- in what we have just seen now, the tape, that there was a common knowledge that Srebrenica was not well defended or defendable. Was this conclusion -- do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I said at the beginning that Srebrenica could have been defended but in a different way, if the combat at the battlefront had been conducted in a different way in the theatre of war of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, the strategy of warfare should have been different and not of the kind that it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, just to see, first you said that -- in your report that the weapons in Srebrenica represented no threat inside and, of course, it was demilitarised as much as possible. Was that also known by the Bosnian Serb party, that there was so little weapons in Srebrenica, that it was not among the priorities of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I think they knew. I think they knew what kind of military potential Srebrenica had, and I also think they knew that this did not pose a threat to their own security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What makes you think so?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: The Srebrenica enclave is deep in the rear and was surrounded by Serb forces; therefore, at the time of demilitarisation, they knew the materiel and equipment that Srebrenica had, approximately. And the soldiers were able to assess what quantity of weapons had been given to them from the demilitarisation period to July 1995. On the basis of that, they knew that they were no threat to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But apart from this military knowledge, do you think there was also some common knowledge, and you are not -- you don't need to answer my question, it was common knowledge that -- which is just the conclusion I drew from the tape and from what we were hearing, that there was some kind of tendency to give up Srebrenica for a broader solution for peace, that's one thing we heard; that the authorities were ready to exchange Srebrenica for other Muslim territories, apparently five territories along the Drina; and the fact that fighters were taken away, the best fighters were taken away. Was there some kind, in your opinion, the political side knew that Srebrenica is really not defendable, the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that Naser Oric and 18 officers were undergoing training in Zenica, that was common knowledge in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Bosnian public was opposed to this kind of policy and opposed to the division of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in this, public opinion was tested, and it was a sort of preparation for what was to happen, what was to occur later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think I have finished my questions. Thank you very much, General Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. General Halilovic, at the time of the 1995 Srebrenica attack, after Naser Oric and his top people had left, who was in charge of the remaining forces of the BiH army, the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: From the documents that I had access to, General Rasim Delic, after maybe a month of time, appointed Ramiz Becirevic, a Major with the BH army, to be the deputy commander or the representative of the commander of the 28th Division. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Becirevic was on the spot, he was in the area of Srebrenica, at this time, at the time of the siege, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I gather from your prior remarks, but let me make sure that I understood them correctly; is it your feeling, based upon your interviews and your reading, that the remaining forces of the 28th Division in and around the Srebrenica enclave, that they were capable or incapable of putting up a strong resistance without the reinforcement from other parts of the Bosnian army? We talked about your criticism of the strategy of concentrating on Sarajevo, but the forces that were actually there in July, could they have resisted the attack or would it have been militarily hopeless?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: If we should look at the Srebrenica enclave separately, taken out of context of the overall theatre of operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if those units were to defend themselves on their own, I can only conclude that it would have been very difficult for them to defend themselves on their own. However, in a coordinated action of all of the units within the enclave and the free territory, with the support of the International Community, I think that Srebrenica could have been defended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that very well, but I asked the question because you had made the remark - I don't know whether now it was in your testimony today or quoted in one of the articles - that there were more people acting as security at one of the SDA meetings than there were actually Serbs entering Srebrenica. But I now have your answer to that. Let me ask you further about whether or not you knew whether elements of the Muslim army knew about what was happening in Potocari on the next days, the days after the fall, on the 12th and 13th, the entire evacuation of the women and children, the separation of the men there. To your knowledge, was this something that the army knew, since we've already had testimony in this proceeding that, you know, there were films of it, various people saw it on TV, et cetera? So do you know whether the army knew, and if so, if they had any position on it or whether they did anything about it? I'm now talking about the post-Srebrenica evacuation in Potocari, the events of the 12th and 13th, prior to the executions, just the Potocari part.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: As to what was happening on the 12th and the 13th of July, 1995 in Srebrenica, I learned about that later on from the media. Whether the army was aware of what was happening during those days, I think that General Enver Hadzihasanovic, who is to take the stand after me in this courtroom, will be in a better position to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that. I understand that General Hadzihasanovic will be able to tell us firsthand about many things, but we also value your opinion as somebody who had a background and has since talked to knowledgeable people. So to the extent that you do feel comfortable in answering the questions, I, at least, would value your opinion on that. With respect to this question, we've seen films and had a lot of evidence about the fact that General Mladic, at the Hotel Fontana, when he was negotiating with the DutchBat General Colonel Koroman, et cetera, kept asking for representatives of the Bosnian army to come and negotiate with him. Whether that was done in good faith or not is a different matter, but the fact is he was saying, "Well, bring me somebody from the army. Bring me somebody from the army," and of course nobody from the army came. So I was interested in whether, even later on, after it was all over and you had a chance to talk to people in the Bosnian army, whether there was a strategy by which they either didn't -- they either didn't know about what was happening in Potocari or they had a strategy why they wished not to enter into any of the negotiations about the removal of the civilian population. It's a long question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I want to believe that they didn't know what was happening in Potocari on the 12th and the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I only have one very brief question on the column, which you've already been questioned about. Were you able to find out or come to a conclusion, based upon your interviews and your reading material, as to whether or not when the column was formed - and we've had much evidence about the fact that the front part of the column was the military, the middle part were the civilians - whether -- at whose initiative or who made the recommendation that there should be a column, as opposed to, for instance, the men joining up with the women and going to Potocari, or something else? Do you have any idea who made the decision to form a column? The army people were at the head of the column. I think that's pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to learn from the testimony of the people who were there, and also from the media, immediately prior to the decision about the formation of the column and the direction it was to take, there was a meeting of the military and political leadership who were in Srebrenica, and I think that it was them who actually reached that decision. And I think that afterwards they simply informed others that they were about to leave, and then the communication was switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that, from some of your interviews, that the Bosnian Herzegovina army did not know the direction in which the column was moving until, I guess, some actually arrived near Tuzla. I'd be interested in your opinion about that, because we have heard testimony here that, for instance, the Serbian, the Bosnian Serbs, picked up the information about the column as early as the morning of July 12th. We have intercepts to that effect. We also have people who saw movies of people being captured from the column and standing on the Sandici fields in Belgrade, and even as far away as China, suggesting that during that week lots of people -- by the couple of days the UN was starting to put out -- the UN representative of human rights was starting to put out documents, Security Council was starting to have meetings. It's just difficult to understand why the Bosnian army wouldn't know the direction that the column was moving. Do you have any thoughts on that?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: The claim that the Bosnian army was not aware of the direction in which the column was moving is -- I must admit, seems to be an unreliable one. They must have known. They should have informed themselves about the direction of the column, and they should have taken measures in order to help them. So that claim seems unconvincing to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know, following along on that, whether or not anybody or any forces in the Bosnian army ever had discussions with the Serbian army about what happened to the so-called missing Muslim men from Srebrenica? Now, this would probably have had to be toward the end of the week or maybe even after the major massacres were already completed, but do you know whether or not there were ever discussions held between the Bosnian army and their counterparts on the Bosnian Serb side as to what happened to the men? And I refer you, for instance, to several pieces of testimony we've had here where General Mladic is reported to have been addressing groups of the Muslim men prior to their execution on fields, and saying to them, "Your own people don't want you, and so therefore I'll have to take care of you." This was after prior declarations by Mladic to earlier groups that, "We'll exchange you for," you know, "on prisoner exchange." Do you know anything about whether or not there were, in fact, any discussions during that week, or soon thereafter, about exchanges of prisoners or what had happened to the missing men?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You never heard, even later on, that there were any such discussions about prisoner exchange or what happened to those particular men? Okay. I just have one or two very brief questions to finish up.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I would be interested in your views, if you care to present them, based upon your own study of these events, as to what factors you believe might have led the -- whoever is responsible on the other side to actually execute these thousands of Muslim men following the fall of Srebrenica, considering that the later -- after Zepa, there was an orderly, a reasonably orderly withdrawal of all the forces, and that Srebrenica stands out as a somewhat unusual, in its scope and horror, event?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Methodologically speaking, Srebrenica is no different from some other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is true that it is significantly different in terms of the number of the people that were executed. As to why it took place in the Drina River valley, I think the reasons can be found in the decisions issued by the Serbian Assembly in Banja Luka, which I mentioned at the beginning of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Why would that -- I can understand that might account for siege of Srebrenica and maybe even the evacuation of the people, but why kill all these people as opposed to putting them in prisons and exchanging them later and even putting them in camps, as we well know - we have lots of experience with detention camps - but the immediate executions, which were, at least so far as we know, have been unusual.

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that today there are more than 60 settlements consisting of Bosniak population mainly who wish to go back to their homes, but those who were executed no longer have any chance of going back home, and that area was removed from the face of the earth. It was cleansed, and as an area which was between two Serb states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, my final one: Did you, in any of your interviews or your perusal of materials, find out whether or not the Bosnian army was ever aware later on in September and October of 1995 of these reburials of some of the mass graves that were going on in the same area, and if so, whether they had any position or took any action thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot say whether the BH army had any knowledge about that. I learnt about it by watching satellite footage which was very graphic in its presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When did you see that satellite footage, approximately when?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I think a year or two after Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So at the immediate time, and I'm sure you followed newspapers and media because you were interested in the events, but at the immediate time in September and October, you didn't have any awareness of those reburials going on?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: September, October, if you're referring to 1995 --

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: -- then I didn't have any knowledge about that at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. General Halilovic, I should like to go back to the agreement of the demilitarisation of the enclave. In view of the provisions of that agreement which you have discussed, the agreement of the 17th of April, 1993, General Morillon, General Mladic, and yourself, since you were the signatories of this agreement, what did you mean by the term "demilitarisation" itself? What was the interpretation which was given to that term?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: According to the agreement on the demilitarisation, the term is understood to mean demilitarisation of the urban area of Srebrenica and Zepa towns, as well as the immediate surrounding area which could be seen with the naked eye. No individuals under arms could be found in that area, nor could there be any presence of any weaponry in the area. If anyone wanted to enter the safe area, he was supposed to leave the weapons at the entrance into the area. So, the term "demilitarised area" implied the urban areas of those two towns and the immediate surrounding zone around that urban area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there a definition of the urban area contained in the agreement?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: The agreement I told you about specified that there would be a three-member commission which would -- the representatives of the UNPROFOR would be in charge of delineating the demilitarised area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that this issue has to a certain extent already been discussed, but I should like to know whether the agreement envisaged any violations, and in cases of violations, were any sanctions envisaged or provided for by the agreement?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no specific provisions to that effect in the agreement; however, it was implied that it was a -- since it was a two-party agreement which was signed under the auspices of UNPROFOR, that if either of the parties is not satisfied with the implementation of the agreement, that they could always withdraw the signature, their signature, on the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me go back to another issue. The transfer of 18 officers who were based in Srebrenica and who were under Naser Oric to undergo training in Zenica, how are we to understand the term "training"; literally or other? What is the exact meaning of the term that you used in respect of those officers?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: In the order whereby they were sent for further education, it was stated that they were to be sent to school, to training or education, and that indeed happened; but it is my opinion that those who were in charge of that order should have been aware of the consequences of such a move, that is, that the combat readiness and capability, defence capability of Srebrenica would be significantly affected. I would never have issued such an order. I would have done something completely different. I would have sent 18 capable people over there to Srebrenica and not move them out of Srebrenica, to teach them what they needed to know over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does it mean that it is your opinion that there was a connection between that particular decision and the attack?

utterances.speaker: SEFER HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that one can conclude from what I have already said that there is, indeed, a connection between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we have any more questions for you, General. Let me thank you very much, General Halilovic, for coming here to testify and for having contributed to the clarification of these very important issues. I should like to wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence and a lot of success in your work. Thank you once again. Mr. Usher, could you please accompany the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours. I just wanted to ask if there was any possibility for me to go back tomorrow because there is a return of population to the Podrinje area going on at this time, and that was the reason why I made that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General, it is possible for you to go back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we can now continue with our next witness, General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General Hadzihasanovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please read the solemn declaration that the usher is giving to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated now. So, General Hadzihasanovic, let me say for the record, that is, let me ask you for the record to spell out your name.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Enver Hadzihasanovic, and I'm a retired army General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 7th of July, 1950, in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current position?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I am a General of the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, retired, a retired General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where exactly do you live now, in which town?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I live in Sarajevo in Trampina Street, number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we proceed with your testimony, properly speaking, let me first of all thank you on behalf of the Chamber for having responded to the summons we issued for you, and for having accepted to place yourself at our disposal by appearing before the Chamber in this case. Thank you very much for the very detailed letter that you addressed to the Chamber with a number of attachments. I would like to say something about the general framework of your testimony. You have been invited to testify as a court witness in this case, whereas in other cases, normally it is the parties to the case who usually call their witnesses. It is my duty as the president of this Chamber to remind you briefly of the conditions under which your testimony will take place. I know that you are familiar with the procedure that we are going to apply, but let me remind you once again of the overall conditions. I know that you have already appeared as a witness before the Tribunal, before a Chamber that I had the honour to be part of. You have been summoned to tell the whole truth and nothing but the truth in this case. The sessions are public in principle, and we should like to preserve that public character of the hearing as much as it is possible. However, should you deem it necessary, you can always ask the Chamber to order a private or a closed session which, in practical terms, means that for as long as the closed session or the private session lasts, the public are not be able to hear your words, and the transcript of your testimony during that period of time will not be made public. If you have any notes, you may use them to refresh your memory, but we would like to ask you not to read a written statement that you may have compiled in advance. We should like to hear your spontaneous narrative about the events that you are familiar with concerning the attack against the Srebrenica enclave by Serb forces in July 1995, the fall, the subsequent fall of that enclave, and the destiny of the civilian and military population of the area. After that, you will probably receive questions from the parties, and after their questions, the Judges will also probably have a few questions for you. You may refuse to respond to a question, you have the right to do that; however, I have to advise you that you may do so only if your response is likely to incriminate you in accordance with the provisions of Rule 90 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Judges can oblige you to answer the question anyway, but such an answer of yours can never be used in evidence against yourself. Let me also inform you that we usually make a break after one hour and 20 minutes of testimony, but I don't think that that will be necessary now. We may work a little later today, but we will see about that. Thank you very much for your attention. I hope that I was clear and that you have understood me well, and let me now ask you if you are ready to proceed with your testimony, that is, if you can proceed with telling us something about your career, in particular, in the period of time which followed the year 1993. You have the floor, General.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm ready to begin. First of all, I should like to say good afternoon to the Trial Chamber and to thank them for their hospitality here in The Hague. Let me say that as a military man, I will be speaking about military matters. I don't wish to enter into questions of a political nature; that is not my field. Of course, what I say, I say publicly. I have no request for any other kind of sessions but public ones. I can commence, but I think it would be easier for me, perhaps, if you, Mr. President, were to ask questions and thus guide my presentation so that you hear what you wish to hear from me at this -- these proceedings. I will start in the way that I think would be a good idea, and I will focus on the main events. In 1993, at the end of 1993, in October more specifically, I took on the duty of the Chief of Staff of the General Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I remained in that post until 1995, the end of 1995, when the Dayton Accords were signed, and when, according to those accords, it was necessary to establish the army of the federation, and General Dudakovic took over from me. For one -- I had a pause for one year because I had a traffic accident myself and I was on sick leave because I had received an injury to my leg. I took up my duties again in the Ministry of Defence when I came back from sick leave, and I was the deputy assistant of the Ministry of Defence in the federation for inspection and supervision affairs. And last year in April, I retired as -- I was pensioned as a General. That, briefly, is my curriculum vitae since 1993. I should like to start off by saying something about the 28th Division for me to be able to base my further presentation on this, which was -- and it was located in Srebrenica. I'm not going to take up too much of the Court's time with facts and details because I can hand some documents over to the Court for its use, and one of those documents, which is in three parts, is the structure and organisation of the 28th Division itself, how it was established militarily speaking, and what we thought that informational terms, establishment terms, it was to be organised, how it should be armed, and how it should be established, the army and that division. And that was their basic document according to which they were to function. In 1993 and 1994, we had series reorganisation in the BH army, and we organised the brigades and corps according to the standards as we set them out. It was our great problem how we could do this with the 8th Operative Group that we had up until then in Srebrenica because, in fact, it was a component part of the 2nd Corps of the BH army, and that problem is something that the command of the 2nd Corps wanted us to solve, and the only way of doing this was that we established with the 28th Division the proper communication, which we did not have up until that time. We had a modest means of communication, and when I say that, I mean an amateur radio station where we were only able to open -- to talk about the vital day-to-day questions and issues openly. But in order to be able to protect this communication of ours, we had to send special communication devices which would ensure that. And so in the second half of 1994, we succeeded in doing so, with a group of members of the BH army. We took communication devices. One of them was a PC, a computer, a PC. That was one device of the type that is used in that mode of communication. It had a modem for encryption and so on. And from Srebrenica we got a written paper, and this allowed us to send out written documents. So that is how we sent the documents that I'm able to provide you with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, perhaps we could talk about communication. Did the Bosniak authorities -- were they put up-to-date regularly of the events taking place in the Srebrenica enclave? And perhaps you could add the military situation and the forces that were in place.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I was going on to explain, Mr. President. I said up until then it was the 8th Operative Group, and its structure and organisation did not entirely correspond to the structure and organisation of the BH army itself. And we wanted to put that matter right, to correct it, because without means of communication, we were not able to send out these three documents which I have here. The first document relates to the structure and organisation of the command of divisions. The second document relates to the structure and organisation of one light brigade, and the 28th Division in Srebrenica had five of -- five formations of that type. Zepa too belonged to that division, militarily and organisationally speaking, where one brigade was put up. And the division had a light battalion, and this document is the groundwork for those formations. For us to send this out, we had to send people on foot to actually take these communication devices and to establish communication with them. When this was received, the division was able to become established on the basis of that document, with respect to manpower mostly rather than technical materiel, which was always lacking; it was always in short supply. As far as manpower went, the figures -- the numbers are as follows, the strength of the forces was as follows. If the Court requires these documents, I shall be happy to furnish them. I hope that I won't use up too much time, but I shall have to comment. May I avail myself of that opportunity? May I go ahead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Hadzihasanovic. You may use those documents, but let us start out from the point of view that the public, in fact, has no knowledge of those documents. Please bear that in mind and proceed. I don't know whether the two parties wish to have the document. Mr. Harmon, let us hear you first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the witness is going to use a document in Court, I think it should be given an identification number and an exhibit number, and then we can refer to the exhibit number during the course of the examination, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, what do you have to say on the issue? Mr. Visnjic, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I join the proposal made by Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Hadzihasanovic, in order to be able to organise our discussion -- I don't know whether you have any copies - I don't suppose you do - of that document. Do you have any copies?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: These three documents that I mentioned are very extensive documents, and from them I have made summaries, which I shall be commenting on to save time. The excerpts that I'm going to talk about, I have copies of and can provide them, whereas the documents in their entirety, if you wish to take them to have them photocopied, they are at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have copies, we can have them distributed. But what we need to do is to assign a number for identification, for each document, so that we can refer back to it. If you have copies, you can hand them to the usher, who will distribute them, and if you place the document on the ELMO, that would be a help. And we will assign an identification number to the document. Mr. Usher, please take the document. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a total of four copies. I need one and I can hand three over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I see Mr. Visnjic on his feet. Go ahead, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we agree to the witness using these copies, or excerpts from the documents, but not to lose time, after today's session we should like to have permission to take a look at the original documents, because these -- this document is a summary taken from the original extensive documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Hadzihasanovic, you were going to say something. I interrupted you. I apologise. Please say what you were going to say. No? Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that I have four copies. I need one for myself. Are three copies sufficient for the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. You have three copies, that is to say, four in all, four copies in all. As to the original -- we could give a copy to the Prosecution and the Defence, and the registrar will have the other available copy. As soon as you place a document on the ELMO, we shall be able to follow and we shall assign an identification number to that particular document. So the registrar has a copy, the two parties have a copy, and the registrar will make copies for the Judges. So would you please hand over your copy, one for the Defence and one for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I think that we're ready to begin. Would you place the document on the ELMO. And Madam Registrar will assign a number. What number do we have, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] C-1. Very well. C-1. The Chamber, number 1. General, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to confirm, the documents that I'm going to comment on are the product of the original documents. They are taken from the original documents that went to Srebrenica. According to those documents, the 28th Division in Srebrenica should have had, in total, 5.685 men. That is the total, and it is shown here at the bottom of this column. In actual fact, in Srebrenica it had 5.803 men, and the percentage was 102 per cent, which can be seen down here. On this part of the diagram, you see the structure and organisation of the 28th Division itself in Srebrenica, without the brigade from Zepa. The request by the General Staff of the army was that each unit should have 110-per-cent manpower, a strength of 110 per cent. Here you see that the percentage is 102, but including the Zepa Brigade, which had more men, then the percentage would be 108 per cent, was within allowed limits. I will take this diagram away now and we'll take a look at another diagram relating to manpower. On the basis of these documents, the 28th Division did not have the kind of equipment and weaponry that it should have had, so on this second diagram I'm going to give you the exact figures of what it should have had and what it indeed had. I also have the same number of copies, so I shall hand them over to the usher to distribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Would you mark your own copy. The first document was C-1. This will be document C-2. And you can mark your own document, because you will know which one is yours and which one you have handed to the parties, and you will be able to refer to the document by its identification number, which is C-2.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now have the second document, which is C-2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Document C-2 relates to what was necessary, according to the requests made by the division, what they should have had, and the actual state of affairs, that is to say, what the division in Srebrenica actually disposed of, actually had in its possession. We enumerate the basic types of weaponry which it should have had, so that pistols, for example, in the case of pistols, the division in Srebrenica should have had 1.184 -- no. No. It doesn't seem to be right. I apologise. It's difficult for me to follow on the monitor, on the screen. That's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, are you able to follow on the ELMO? When you point things out to us on the ELMO, it comes out on our monitors, on our screens, so we're able to follow too.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I wasn't getting the whole picture on the monitor. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have it now. It's been adjusted. Thank you. Let me repeat. According to the documents that we sent out, in Srebrenica there should have been 1.184 pistols; what they actually had was 62. Automatic rifles, they should have had 4.109 of them; in actual fact, they had 1.947, or 46 per cent. Sniper rifles, they should have had 128, and in actual fact they only had 13. Submachine-gun, they should have had 326; they actually had 27. Machine-guns, they should have had 90 -- no, 83; in actual fact, they had 15. Mortars, 60-millimetre ones, they should have had 98; in actual fact, they only had 12. 82-millimetre mortars, 36; they had 5. 120-millimetre mortar, they should have had 36; they had none, in actual fact. Hand grenades, hand launchers, 16 they should have had, but they just had 9. Hand-held rocket launchers, that was. Recoilless guns, 82 millimetres, they should have had 36; they had 4. Hand-held rocket launchers of the Zolja type, they should have had 478; they had 68. Anti-armour Osa-type launchers, they should have had 143; they had none. Rocket launchers, hand-held armoured, 9-K-11, they should have had 18; they had none. A light launcher of the Fagot type, 9-K-11-F, they should have had 15 of those; they just had 1. Anti-missile rockets, they should have had 15; they didn't have 1. Anti-aircraft guns of the 20-millimetre type, one barrel, they should have had 20. In actual fact, they only had 4. Along with this column, we have the percentages which you can look at. So that was the actual situation in Srebrenica as to what it should have been on the basis of these documents. At the end of 1994 in Srebrenica, the overall situation was highly complex and extremely difficult, both with respect to the army and the people, and it became even more complex because all humanitarian convoys had been blocked and because the parachute operation undertaken by the United Nations had always been stopped. And there was every indication that in Srebrenica, the worst things could be expected, that people could just leave without thinking, to leave a situation that was untenable for them. And we tried to organise the army and to tell the people that we, ourselves, wanted to take steps to calm the situation down until a final, better solution was -- had been come up with. And so at the request of the division and according to our own assessments, we wanted to help the situation in the army by sending them more resources and to enable that particular division, if there were any serious problems, to ensure its combat readiness to be able to defend themselves in the days to come until we ourselves were able to undertake other steps and military steps if we failed to find a political solution and if the United Nations were not able to carry out what they promised with respect to the safe area. That was our goal. A division organised in this way and established in this way absolutely was no threat to the Serb army or to anybody else in the region. The division as a whole, for it to embark upon a combat operation with the amount of ammunition that it had would have been completely impotent. We knew that we weren't -- would not be able to furnish the division with what it needed quickly because we were not able to get the materiel and resources to them. Our first attempt was to introduce the communication devices, and we decided to do that on the ground, on land, with a certain number of men that we had at our disposal. But that didn't prove successful. The people that we dispatched, that we sent, were sent into a risky situation. They risked being captured and ultimately liquidated if captured. So it was a high-risk situation for the men. And then we decided to do this with the modest means we had at our disposal and the number of helicopters we had at our disposal, the few helicopters we had. In our estimations, this would be a difficult task and would require a lot of time. We were not able to give the pilots an exclusive military order to fly because we knew we would be sending them to their death, and we -- it was on a voluntary, almost a voluntary basis that these sorties were organised. And we sent ten helicopters. The structure of the helicopters included some weapons and some ammunition, but they were also carrying clothing and sanitary material. They also transported a certain number of doctors and brought out some seriously wounded people and people that were supposed to go on for further education. It was probably a signal to the army of Republika Srpska that something was afoot and that they could expect some combat operations; however, I say with full responsibility here and now that that was not our objective. Our objective was to establish an army, to establish a command over the army, and that they should act on the basis of orders and commands, but for us to be able to do that, we had to see that their combat readiness was up to par. For us to be able to do this, we needed a lot more time, and time was something that depended on how far we were able to transport these supplies. I have documents here which indicate how much time we would have needed and how many tons of cargo would have been necessary for the division to receive basic resources, that is to say, ammunition for their rifles, one combat kit for mortars and for the anti-armoured devices, and for everything that they were lacking, in fact. And in order not to waste time now, you can use these documents and the tables, and the next table will, I'm sure, will -- be identified as C-3, and it shows just how much material was necessary for Srebrenica, expressed in tons, for them to be able to receive one combat kit and one unit of fire and the other materiel. I will be happy to supply copies of this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will be document C-3. Perhaps, General, instead of analysing the details on the basis of the table, you could perhaps give us an idea of a more general nature. You could tell us about this in more general terms, and may we have your conclusions on the basis of the document.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will try and do so as briefly as possible. And, of course, if you're interested, you can use this table because these indices and this data was taken from the standards that were applicable in the former JNA, and they emerge from the standards for the resources and equipment that I am talking about. Let me just show you two more diagrams, and then I will give you my conclusions and say what I wanted to say. For the division in Srebrenica, minus one brigade, receive the weapons it lacked, we had to transport a total of 58.4 tons of material. For it to receive the ammunition it needed, this meant an extra 142.6 tons which had to be dispatched and transported. The individual equipment is given on the diagram, and I don't want to comment on that now. At the time, for a division, in terms of weapons and ammunition, this meant something but it did not mean everything, so in the next diagram I wanted to explain that if a minimum of necessary material was to be sent, we had to send a certain quantity expressed in tons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This, then, General, will be C-4, document C-4.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: For the men to have just one meal a day, a cold ration, dry ration, which each soldier has to carry with him when he is on an assignment, we would have to have sent, to supply only that one dry ration, which was two kilograms, an extra 11.6 tons would have had to be transported to ensure two kilograms per man per day. When we're talking about clothing, we did not go -- we did not count clothing, shoes, shirts, trousers, and so on, but just tents, and that meant an additional 8.7 tons. To ensure the means of communication within a division required an additional 2.96 tons to be transported. When we saw how many flights a helicopter would have had to make, this was an enormous number, and I show this on my next diagram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This next document will be numbered C-5.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: In order to transport the necessary materiel, one combat ammunition set which would be necessary for the division to defend itself for a period of three to five days, they would need -- we would need to send out a total of 8 times an escadrille of 6 helicopters, a squad of 6 helicopters, which is something we did not have. For the dry rations and ground canvases and tents, 1 squad plus 2 helicopters, and for all this materiel we would have to have sent 9 squads times 6 helicopters, with 2 helicopters flying independently. For that division to engage in combat, according to our assessments, it would need at least 5 combat ammunition sets and all the squadrons I mentioned. And for that to be ensured, a 6 helicopter squadron would have had to fly 28 times, 28 days, plus 2 individual helicopters flying during that time. Our attempts were made with the 10 helicopters I mentioned in different intervals at the end of 1994 and 1995, and they gave hope to the people over there that something was being done, that we were doing something to help them. And that was our main objective, to give them that hope, although we knew that we could not ensure that many number of flights. We had a total of just 6 helicopters; of that number, 2 MTB 17 were capacitated to take a cargo of 3 tons. All the other helicopters had a lower-bearing capacity. And we achieved our objective. The situation in Srebrenica was calmed down, the people believed in the army more, had a greater belief in the army, and they believed that, if anything happened, the army could protect them. By doing that, we had achieved one of our goals completely, that is to say, the soldiers formed formational structures, they were established, and we started to supply them with the materiel they needed in addition to what they already had. And this calmed the mood in Srebrenica. However, quite unexpectedly, the situation developed, and what happened was the attack on the Srebrenica enclave by the army of Republika Srpska. There were intimations in the early summer of 1995 that this might happen sometime in April and in May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, General, but I think that we'll have to end there for today. We have been working for an hour and a half now, and because of the interpreters and everybody else, we shall have to end there today and take up our deliberations tomorrow morning at 9.20. I'm going to ask Mr. Fourmy, the legal officer, to try to organise the documents, to help you organise the documents so that tomorrow morning we could perhaps proceed with greater speed. We would like to have an overview and a general idea on the basis of the documents but not to go into the details. Yes, they are important for us, but for the public gallery attending these proceedings, we should also like to have a more general view and general conclusions and observations. So I'm going to ask Mr. Fourmy and Madam Registrar to do that together with you. Having said that, we adjourn and reconvene at 9.20 tomorrow morning. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
